structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Excerpt from Santander’s Annual Report 2024, Sustainability Statement, which consolidates non-financial and sustainability information.
- Contents overview signposts the broader report sections: business model and strategy; sustainability statement; corporate governance; economic and financial review; risk management and compliance.
- 2024 sustainability highlights quantify Santander’s economic, social, and environmental impact:
  - EUR 350.5 billion in home financing enabling 3.7 million families to access housing; EUR 214.2 billion in consumer finance.
  - EUR 330 billion to support company setup and growth, including over 530,000 SMEs and self-employed.
  - Workforce of 206,753 employees; EUR 14.3 billion in wages and benefits.
  - EUR 11.6 billion paid to suppliers, 89% of whom are local (88% of procurement turnover).
  - EUR 10.9 billion in taxes paid by the Group and EUR 11.5 billion in third-party taxes collected.

  - 4.3 million people financially included since 2023; microfinance in Latin America reached 1.3 million underbanked entrepreneurs with EUR 1.27 billion disbursed.
  - EUR 166 million in community support, including EUR 104 million for higher education, employability, and entrepreneurship.
- Notes indicate figures largely refer to credit stock and holdings as of 31 December 2024, with SME data based on customers with outstanding loans at year-end.

nodes.title: Sustainability strategy
nodes.heading: 1.1 Sustainability strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Grupo Santander’s purpose is to help people and businesses prosper.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Santander’s sustainability approach and global footprint: purpose to help people and businesses prosper; ambition to be the best open financial services platform; 173+ million customers, 200k+ employees; five global businesses operating across core markets in Europe, North America and South America via a multichannel proposition.
- Sustainability strategy built on a double materiality assessment and five pillars: enabling customer transition to a low‑carbon economy and managing climate risks; developing employees through inclusion, learning and fair work; supporting communities with a focus on education, employability and entrepreneurship; being a trusted partner via responsible products, financial inclusion and data protection; and acting responsibly through strong culture, governance and conduct. Tied to the Group’s Think Value, Think Customer and Think Global action lines, embedded in business strategies and linked to remuneration; governance referenced.
- Business-line ambitions and actions:
  - Retail & Commercial Banking: sustainable propositions for individuals, SMEs and corporates; collaboration with multilateral development banks; portfolio emissions measurement (Spain/UK real estate; Brazil agriculture); target to financially include 5 million people (2023–2025) via microfinance, access and financial education; EUR 400 million for education, employability and entrepreneurship (2023–2026), including Santander Open Academy.
  - Digital Consumer Bank: expand sustainable finance in auto and consumer markets; EUR 6.8 billion EV financing in the year; >12% market share of EV sales in Europe; contributes to 2030 alignment.
  - Corporate & Investment Banking: strategic partner for client transition; focus on clean energy and ClimateTech advisory, structured finance and risk solutions; long‑standing leadership in renewable project finance; exceeded EUR 120 billion green finance (2019–2025) target 18 months early; supports client transition plans in high‑emitting sectors.
  - Wealth Management & Insurance: target EUR 100 billion SRI assets under management by 2025; broad SRI fund and insurance range, themed products (climate, transition, natural capital), customized mandates; enhanced engagement and climate‑aligned voting by Santander Asset Management.
  - Payments: reduce card footprint; 39 million cards acquired in 2024 made of sustainable materials (84% of total; recycled PVC/PLA); exploring transaction footprint calculation and offset options.
- Embedding and risk management: sustainability targets integrated into the three‑year strategic and financial plans and annual budget; CEO‑led planning with review by strategy/executive committee and board; risk “Challenge” process and board‑level oversight; comprehensive risk model including ESG; emerging risks exercises to test resilience.
- Stakeholder engagement: continuous, transparent dialogue informing strategy and plans. Employees (Your Voice engagement survey, Canal Abierto ethics channel, structured relations with unions/works councils); customers (retail NPS and biannual benchmarks with action plans; wholesale relationship‑driven feedback); shareholders/investors (surveys, events, digital channels and senior management access); communities (mass perception surveys, two‑way NGO engagement, and ESCC/Equator Principles assessments). Outcomes of double materiality analysis reviewed by senior management and the board.

nodes.title: Stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: 1.2 Stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: Santander remains in constant dialogue with its stakeholder groups, particularly employees, customers, shareholders and communities, who we engaged as part of our materiality assessments and human rights due diligence, as we outline in this report.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Santander’s 2024 stakeholder engagement approach, results, sustainability affiliations, and double materiality assessment under CSRD:

- Stakeholder engagement framework
  - Principles: transparency, honesty, impartiality; engagement used to inform strategy, financial plans, goals, and customer-centric operations.
  - Employees: three listening mechanisms—Your Voice global survey and local pulses; Canal Abierto confidential ethics channel; ongoing dialogue and formal bodies with employees’ legal representatives, including trade unions and works councils.
  - Customers: retail NPS and competitive benchmarks with action plans; wholesale client feedback via bankers and governance channels; integration into the Think Customer strategic pillar; complaints handling referenced.
  - Shareholders and investors: surveys, events, and direct/digital channels to deepen understanding and access to senior management.
  - Communities: mass perception surveys; two-way engagement with NGOs; environmental and social risk analysis through ESCC policy and Equator Principles.

- 2024 engagement in numbers
  - Employees: 83% participation in Your Voice; 4,437 complaints via ethical channels.
  - Customers: >9.9 million surveys; 681,636 complaints received and resolved/under management.
  - Shareholders & investors: 9,136 retail shareholder perception responses; 157,632 survey/study responses; 229 retail shareholder events; 1,269 institutional investor interactions (109 on ESG).
  - Communities: 158 NGO interactions.

- Engagement with other stakeholders and external positioning
  - Suppliers: embedding ESG standards in tenders; support for assessments and certifications.
  - ESG ratings: MSCI AA maintained; CDP A; Sustainalytics score 17.1 (Low Risk); ISS C+.
  - Regulators/supervisors/industry: active policy dialogue with global and European authorities; 53 regulatory consultations responded to in 2024; collaboration via IIF, EBF, AFME and Santander-hosted forums; context on Brazil’s G20 presidency and COP30.
  - Political parties: strict controls—no donations or in-kind contributions; arm’s-length financing only with executive approval; no debt cancellation; market-rate interest required.

- Key sustainability memberships and initiatives
  - General frameworks: UN Global Compact; UNEP FI and founding signatory of Principles for Responsible Banking; PRI via Santander Asset Management; WBCSD (B4ICA, CFO Network, LEAP); Equator Principles; ICMA (sustainable bonds).
  - Disclosure frameworks: ISSB (IFRS Corporate Champions); TCFD support since 2017.
  - Advocacy forums: leadership in IIF; participation in EBF ESG risk and steering groups; AFME Sustainable Finance SteerCo.

- Double materiality assessment (CSRD/ESRS-aligned)
  - Purpose and scope: group-wide (own operations and value chain) with subsidiary-level assessments feeding into Group results.
  - Outcomes: 32 impacts, risks and opportunities identified across five material ESRS matters—E1 Climate Change; S1 Own Workforce; S3 Affected Communities; S4 Consumers & End-users; G1 Business Conduct—with materiality thresholds (critical/significant/informative/minimal).
  - Time horizon: primarily short-to-medium term (1–5 years), with qualitative validation for long-term stability of results.
  - Integration: connected to top and emerging risk processes and other internal risk exercises; approved by the Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Culture Committee; managed through policies, actions, metrics, and targets.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 1.3 Materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase:
Double materiality assessment underpins our sustainability
strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and context: Excerpt from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report detailing its CSRD/ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment and related governance, linking sustainability topics to impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) and to Group risk management.
- Double materiality results: 32 IROs identified. Five ESRS sustainability matters are material: E1 Climate change, S1 Own workforce, S3 Affected communities, S4 Consumers and end users, G1 Business conduct. Non-material matters (below threshold): E2 Pollution, E3 Water and marine resources, E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems, E5 Resource use & circular economy, S2 Workers in the value chain. Aspects of nature/biodiversity are addressed within the transition plan.
- Materiality scope and method: Group-wide (own operations and value chain) with stakeholder engagement and subsidiary-level assessments informing Group results. Time horizon primarily short-to-medium term (1–5 years), with qualitative confirmation that long-term conclusions would not change. Materiality thresholds defined (critical, significant, informative, minimal). Outputs feed top and emerging risks and other internal risk processes; approved by the Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Cultural Committee.
- E1 Climate change IROs: Positive impacts from supporting renewables and reducing Scope 1–2 emissions; adverse impact risk from financing non-sustainable activities; opportunities in financing transition solutions and customer sustainability offerings; reputational risk tied to climate policy progress.
- S1 Own workforce IROs: Positive impacts on health, safety, inclusion, equal opportunity, learning and fair pay; negative impacts from discrimination, poor conditions, harassment or corruption; risks of conflicts from excessive hours, corruption, or rights infringements.
- S3 Affected communities IROs: Positive impacts via credit provision, sustainable finance, and programs in education/employability/entrepreneurship; negative impacts from financing activities breaching policies or insufficient stakeholder due diligence leading to environmental/social harm.
- S4 Consumers and end users IROs: Positive impacts through inclusive, needs-based products and cybersecurity education; negative impacts from poor complaints handling, inadequate product information, data protection failures, and access barriers; risks of fines, claims, and customer loss from privacy breaches or substandard practices.
- G1 Business conduct IROs: Positive impacts from responsible conduct (including tax contribution), effective ethics/reporting channels, and responsible vendor management; negative impacts from unresolved incidents, lack of continuous improvement, bribery/corruption; risks from vendor resilience/compliance gaps and financial crime/AML failures.
- Governance: Board of Directors sets and approves sustainability strategy; the Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Cultural Committee proposes and oversees implementation. Other board committees address specific topics; the Audit Committee oversees financial and non-financial reporting and internal controls aligned with COSO. Material issues and action plans are periodically reviewed across governance bodies.

nodes.title: Sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 1.4 Sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: We manage and review progress with sustainability at the highest level of the business.
nodes.summary:
- Business conduct commitments and risks: acting responsibly toward investors, employees, society and the environment; safeguarding confidentiality in ethical channels; promoting vendor ESG practices; key risks include operational resilience across the value chain, improper conduct (e.g., money laundering), and bribery/corruption.
- Materiality outcomes: five topics deemed non-material (pollution; water and marine resources; biodiversity and ecosystems; resource and circular economy; workers in the value chain), with nature/biodiversity aspects addressed where linked to climate objectives.
- Sustainability governance: board-level oversight of the sustainability agenda and strategy; dedicated Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Cultural Committee; Audit Committee oversight of financial and non-financial reporting and internal control aligned with COSO; risk and compliance committees’ involvement; periodic review of material issues through defined governance bodies.
- Three lines of defense: clear allocation of responsibilities across business owners and sustainability function (1st), risk and compliance (2nd), and Internal Audit (3rd); coordination between risk and sustainability committees on ESG-related conduct risk, data protection, customer vulnerability, reputational issues, and policy adoption.
- Integration of sustainability into incentives: ESG embedded in variable remuneration; LTI schemes for top executives carry a 20% ESG weighting; short-term incentives include a ±5% qualitative sustainability component; in 2024, 8% of the Chairwoman/CEO’s variable pay tied to sustainability and 2% of total pay tied to climate actions.
- ESG performance areas for incentives: inclusive culture and accessibility; financial inclusion and social initiatives; sustainable finance and SRI; progress on climate transition plan toward net zero; and governance enablers (double materiality, policies, data quality).
- Human rights due diligence: board-approved policy commitment; processes to protect employees’ rights, customers’ data and responsible practices, ESCC assessment in client transactions, and supplier management; use of ethical channel (Canal Abierto) to identify and address incidents; comprehensive 2024 due diligence aligned with international frameworks (UN, ILO, OECD), informing the double materiality assessment and strategy.
- Climate transition plan strategy: climate identified as material; three pillars—(1) support customers’ transition (achieved EUR 120bn green finance target early; targeting EUR 220bn by 2030; SRI AuM target of EUR 100bn by 2025), (2) embed climate/environmental factors in risk management with focus on most material sectors, (3) aim to align portfolios with Paris Agreement via 2030 sector targets and asset management alignment.
- Own operations: ongoing efficiency measures and commitment to source 100% renewable electricity by 2025.
- Stakeholder engagement: collaboration with customers/investors through tailored products and tools; participation in climate alliances and working groups; engagement with regulators and policymakers; and community initiatives addressing climate, biodiversity, and social impact.

structure.title: OUR CLIMATE TRANSITION PLAN (Environmental information)
structure.heading: 2. OUR CLIMATE TRANSITION PLAN (Environmental information)
structure.start_phrase: Santander considers climate a material topic, having identified impacts, risks and opportunities in the double materiality assessment.
structure.summary:
- The section outlines Santander’s Climate Transition Plan and strategy, confirming climate as a material topic via a double materiality assessment and meeting legal disclosure requirements.
- The plan is built on three pillars:
  1) Supporting customers’ transition: providing guidance, advice, and products; achieving EUR 120bn in green finance (2019–2025) 18 months early; targeting EUR 220bn by 2030; aiming for EUR 100bn in SRI assets under management by 2025.
  2) Embedding climate in risk management: adopting a risk-based approach focused on the most material sectors; integrating climate and environmental risks across the risk management cycle; using materiality assessments to inform strategy.
  3) Aligning activity with the Paris Agreement: setting 2030 portfolio alignment targets for high-emissions sectors (seven targets across five sectors) and asset management; reducing own operational impact with efficiency measures and sourcing 100% renewable electricity by 2025.
- Stakeholder engagement is central, involving:
  • Customers and investors: tailored products/services, collaborative financing networks, and assessment tools to track transition progress.  
  • Key climate actors: participation in local and international alliances and working groups.  
  • Authorities: engagement with regulators and policymakers on relevant climate agenda developments.  
  • Communities: support for local initiatives on climate change, biodiversity, and social impact.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Santander considers climate a material topic, having identified impacts, risks and opportunities in the double materiality assessment.
nodes.summary:
- Document scope: Extract from Santander’s Annual Report 2024 detailing “Our Climate Transition Plan” (Environmental information), including strategy, ambition, objectives, milestones, and customer support for the transition.
- Strategic approach (three pillars):
  - Support customers’ transition with advice, solutions, and products; achieved EUR 120 bn green finance target 18 months early; new goal EUR 220 bn by 2030; aim for EUR 100 bn SRI AuM by 2025.
  - Embed climate and environmental factors into risk management via a risk-based approach focused on most material sectors, informed by a double materiality assessment.
  - Align portfolios with the Paris Agreement by setting 2030 sector targets in high-emission sectors and reducing own operational footprint; target 100% renewable electricity by 2025.
- Stakeholder engagement: Collaboration with customers/investors, climate alliances, regulators/policymakers, and communities to enable financing, develop tools, and support local initiatives with environmental and social benefits.
- Ambition: Net zero carbon emissions by 2050; highlights the need for supportive incentive frameworks and macroeconomic/public policy alignment to scale transition activity.
- Objectives and KPIs (2019–2025/2030):
  - Green finance raised/facilitated: EUR 139.4 bn by 2024; targets EUR 120 bn by 2025 (met early) and EUR 220 bn by 2030.
  - SRI AuM target: EUR 100 bn by 2025.
  - Thermal coal-related power & mining: phase-out to EUR 0 by 2030.
  - Portfolio alignment targets (2030): emissions intensity for power generation (0.11 tCO2e/MWh), aviation (61.71 gCO2e/RPK), steel (1.07 tCO2e/tS), auto manufacturing (103 gCO2/vkm), auto lending in Europe (75–89 gCO2e/vkm), and absolute emissions for oil & gas (16.98 mtCO2e).
  - Operations: 100% renewable electricity by 2025 in core markets; ongoing Scope 1–2 reductions and residual offsetting; elimination of single-use plastics in core markets’ offices.
  - Methodology: Financed emissions calculated using an internal approach aligned with PCAF.
- 2024 progress highlights:
  - Expanded financed emissions disclosures to residential mortgages (Spain) and commercial real estate (Spain, UK).
  - Continued operational emissions management and plastics phase-out; maintained high share of renewable electricity (96% in 2024).
- Key milestones timeline:
  - Net zero ambition and initial alignment targets (thermal coal, power generation, SAM).
  - Additional targets disclosed for oil & gas, steel, aviation; later extended to automotive manufacturing and lending.
  - Development of the Sustainable Finance and Investment Classification System (SFICS), including transition finance criteria.
  - Financed emissions disclosure extended to UK mortgages and Brazilian agriculture.
  - SAM objective to halve net emissions for 50% of in-scope AuM; plan for 100% renewable electricity use in buildings; continued thermal coal phase-out.
- Supporting customers’ transition (Section 2.2):
  - Growth plan for green finance through strategy execution, SFICS rollout, greenwashing risk controls, data/measurement infrastructure, and trained commercial teams.
  - Identification of transition finance opportunities across key sectors; integration into materiality assessment.
  - EU Taxonomy alignment: green assets ratio 3.28% in 2024 (vs. 2.6% in 2023); taxonomy-aligned assets include EUR 28.1 bn in mortgages and EUR 8.8 bn in auto.
- Asset management (SAM) opportunities: capitalizing on new climate solutions, lower-emission energy sources with policy support, and efficiency gains that reduce costs and enhance asset values.
- Just transition focus: Commitment to an inclusive transition, integrating social considerations into SFICS and risk policies, with attention to regional/sector contexts (e.g., Amazon biome) and participation in initiatives like the Just Transition Alliance.
- CIB performance: EUR 139.4 bn in green finance raised and facilitated (2019–2024), focused on green use-of-proceeds products; on track for EUR 220 bn by 2030.

nodes.title: Supporting our customers in their transition goals
nodes.heading: 2.2 Supporting our customers in their transition goals
nodes.start_phrase: To achieve our net-zero ambition, our main lever as a bank is supporting our customers in their efforts to transition to a low-carbon economy.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines how Santander is embedding sustainability across its businesses, focusing on financing the low‑carbon transition, developing green products, partnering with clients and institutions, and integrating ESG into risk management.

Key themes and highlights:
- Strategy and governance for green finance
  - Main lever to achieve net-zero is supporting customers’ transition through an enhanced sustainable finance and advisory proposition.
  - Three pillars: grow green finance with a clear strategy and value proposition; build Group-wide infrastructure (SFICS classification, greenwashing controls, data strategy); deploy trained commercial teams.
  - Emphasis on a just and inclusive transition, incorporating regional and sector specificities, integrating Just Transition principles into policies and SFICS, and supporting initiatives like the Just Transition Alliance.
  - European Taxonomy alignment: green asset ratio of 3.28% in 2024 (vs. 2.6% in 2023); aligned assets include EUR 28.1 bn in mortgages and EUR 8.8 bn in auto.
  - Asset management identifies climate opportunities in new climate solutions, lower-emission energy sources, and efficient resource use.

- Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB)
  - EUR 139.4 bn in green finance raised/facilitated since 2019; target EUR 220 bn by 2030.
  - 2024 product mix (EUR bn): green bonds 6.9; financial advice 6.0; project finance 5.7; M&A 5.0; export finance 0.3; project bonds 0.2; ECM 0.0. Data sourced from public league tables; not equivalent to EU Taxonomy metrics.
  - Leadership in renewable energy finance: 82 transactions closed in 2024, 4.54% market share (Infralogic).
  - Impact: 10.2 GW greenfield and 28.2 GW brownfield renewable capacity financed/advised in 2024; greenfield capacity can power 6.5 million households annually.
  - Client climate tiering and bespoke advisory to accelerate low‑carbon technologies.
  - Selected transactions: Enel/Masdar PV portfolio stake sale; Canadian Solar’s Recurrent Energy minority sale; Sonnedix EUR 2.5 bn portfolio refinancing; Brazil’s Babilonia Central 554 MW wind for ArcelorMittal; Zunder EUR 225 mn green loan for ultra‑fast EV charging; DCM deals for Saint‑Gobain, A.P. Møller‑Mærsk, Gatwick SLB; Latin America ESG bonds including COFIDE, Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico’s first taxonomy‑aligned bond; export finance for Verkor’s Dunkirk gigafactory; H2GS green steel plant (EUR 3.3 bn) with ECA cover; green guarantees for Siemens Gamesa; sustainability‑linked supply chain finance with Vestas. Multiple industry awards.

- Retail and Commercial Banking
  - Strengthened green offerings in real estate, mobility, agriculture, and circular economy; use of SLLs and products aligned to transition needs.
  - Robust greenwashing risk controls via SFICS, ESG certification forums, and Green Product Inventories.
  - Market initiatives:
    - Spain: energy efficiency loans for homeowners’ associations; Recovery and Resilience Mechanism credit line for EVs, renewables, circular economy, social housing.
    - Brazil: Energía Plus with Holu Solar; FIT Energía marketplace for renewable energy procurement.
    - Poland: “My electric car” program; BGK‑backed green loans; Santander New Energy platform for SMEs.
    - UK: partnerships with Scottish Power and Octopus Energy for solar and heat pumps.
    - Portugal: joined SIBS to help SMEs manage and disclose ESG data.
    - Argentina: Tienda GRO marketplace for financing sustainable products; expanded retail solar partnerships.
    - Chile: first IFC‑aligned real estate loan under EDGE Advanced; Tesla partnership.
    - Uruguay/Argentina: world’s largest electric ferry financing with IFC participation.
    - Peru: trade finance for a GlobalG.A.P.-certified exporter.
    - Colombia: financing for electric forklifts; solar partnership with Enel X.

- Collaboration with multilateral institutions
  - Participation in InvestEU’s Green Gateway Advisory Programme to align eligibility and unlock MDB tools.
  - Synthethic securitization with EIB in Portugal enabling discounted loans for near‑zero‑emission new buildings and sustainable renovations.

- Wealth Management & Insurance
  - SAM’s SRI range: Article 8 funds (1–50% sustainable investment objective) and Article 9 funds (up to 100% excluding cash/derivatives).
  - Thematic funds in renewables, social, agriculture, and climate; flagship Santander Sostenible Bonos in green/social/climate bonds.
  - Private markets: SAI strategies in Iberian renewables and climate tech (Innoenergy Climate Fund).
  - Advisory for LA Green blended finance fund to catalyze SME green bonds in Latin America.
  - Expanded solidarity funds donating fees to NGOs; award recognition for solidarity initiatives.

- Digital Consumer Bank (SCF)
  - Auto: EUR 6.8 bn EV financing in 2024; 243,315 EVs financed (17% of business); 12% EV market share in Europe; EVs are 24% of new car agreements. Context on EU emissions targets and 2035 ICE sales ban; market sensitivity to subsidies and infrastructure constraints.
  - Partnerships with EV OEMs and traditional manufacturers; innovative bundles (home chargers, solar).
  - Non‑auto: green finance models for solar and efficient home systems, EV charging, micromobility, circular economy (e.g., recycled cards, device buybacks), and education financing. “Hazte ECO” card initiative donates 1% of purchases to environmental projects. EUR 155 mn green finance disbursed in 2024; notes consumer barriers and the importance of subsidies.

- Payments
  - 84% of newly acquired cards (39 million) made from recycled/sustainable materials; tools to estimate and offset card‑based carbon footprints.

- ESG in risk management (Section 2.3)
  - ESG factors embedded across credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, and strategic risks with a risk‑based, materiality‑driven approach emphasizing climate and nature.
  - Transition risk channels: market sentiment, policy actions (e.g., carbon pricing, efficiency, water/land use), and technology shifts.
  - Physical risk: acute (extreme events) and chronic (temperature rise, drought, sea level, variability).
  - Beyond climate: nature‑related risk from biodiversity loss and ecosystem service degradation.
  - Social risk managed via internal policies aligned with international standards; governance risk assessed both internally and for clients.

nodes.title: Embedding ESG in risk management
nodes.heading: 2.3 Embedding ESG in risk management
nodes.start_phrase: Due to our ESG strategy, the scrutiny from stakeholders and the regulatory, reporting and disclosure requirements, we continue to work on embedding and monitoring ESG aspects in risk management.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from Banco Santander’s 2024 Annual Report (Risk management and compliance) detailing how ESG—especially climate and environmental factors—are embedded across the Group’s risk framework, strategy, governance, and disclosures. Includes sections 2.3 (ESG in risk management), 2.3.1–2.3.5 (resilience, risk cycle, reputational risk, financial effects, nature/biodiversity), SAM’s approach, and 2.4 (Paris Agreement alignment).

- Risk taxonomy and drivers:
  - Climate risks categorized as Transition Risk (market sentiment, policy action, technology) and Physical Risk (acute events like floods/wildfires; chronic changes like heat, sea level rise, rainfall shifts).
  - “Beyond climate” natural risk: biodiversity loss and ecosystem service degradation.
  - ESG factors treated as cross-cutting, potentially impacting credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, and strategic risks.

- Time horizons and scenarios:
  - Present/short/medium/long-term assessments aligned to portfolio maturities.
  - Scenario sets: NGFS (Orderly, Disorderly, Hot House World) and IPCC RCPs (2.6/4.5/8.5).

- Risk-by-risk potential impacts, actions, and next steps:
  - Credit: Higher defaults, collateral devaluation, sector sentiment shifts, higher costs for carbon-intensive clients; actions include portfolio materiality assessments, climate concentration monitoring, heatmaps, scenario analysis affecting PD/LGD, risk appetite limits, integration of environmental & climate change (E&CC) factors in ratings; next steps include broader rollout of “The Climate Race” operating model and enhanced internal climate models.
  - Market: Spread widening and volatility for climate-exposed sectors; ongoing climate stress testing and trading book analysis; plan to enhance scenarios and align to market practice.
  - Liquidity: Potential HQLA valuation impacts and funding stresses in climate events; scenario comparisons show impacts below standard liquidity stress tests; further scenario enhancement planned.
  - Operational: Facilities/business continuity risks from severe weather; legal/compliance and greenwashing-related losses; controls include ESG flags in loss data, scenario analysis, BCP integration, training; plans to expand reporting, industry cooperation, and insurance analyses.
  - Reputational: Stakeholder scrutiny of climate policies, financing choices, disclosures, and greenwashing; governance through preventative measures, monitoring, working groups, and greenwashing guidance; aim to deepen integration and quantification of reputational impacts.
  - Strategic: Risks to achieving climate targets and navigating divergent regulations; regular KPI monitoring, emerging risk analysis, governance oversight; continued alignment checks.

- Resilience and integration into the risk cycle:
  - End-to-end embedding of climate/environmental factors across identification, planning, assessment, monitoring, mitigation, and reporting.
  - Use of recognized sources (TCFD, UNEP FI, ENCORE, SBTN, NGFS) and tools (heatmaps, sector classifications, scenarios).
  - Consolidated materiality assessment with RAG status across time horizons; 2024 enhancements improve regulatory alignment, granularity, and cross-risk consistency.

- Tools, models, and analytics:
  - Klima tool centralizes ESCC credit risk materiality, sector/geography views, physical risk on activities and collateral.
  - Vulnerability heatmaps (NACE levels up to 4) provide forward-looking sector/geography risk.
  - Internal climate models quantify PD/LGD impacts via bottom-up (client) and top-down (sector/region) approaches, integrating NGFS and RCP pathways; include counterparty financial forecasts and Frye–Jacobs PD–LGD linkage.
  - Physical risk analytics with a reinsurance partner across 13 hazards for >1,250 regions; EU granularity improved to postcode in Spain, Portugal, UK, Poland.
  - Real estate: Expanded EPC data capture and ML estimation; portfolio module covers transition and physical risk; EPC coverage and distribution tracked.
  - Auto consumer: Deep-dive on technology mix, residual values, maturities, sentiment/regulatory shifts.

- Governance, monitoring, and policies:
  - Risk appetite metrics expanded from coal/mining/power to oil & gas, steel, aviation, and automotive (including SCF Auto) with 2025 rollouts.
  - ESG Regulatory Radar tracks evolving rules; investment and product governance forums review ESG aspects.
  - Climate Community shares best practices and implementation guidance.
  - ESCC risk policy sets sector standards, prohibited and enhanced-due-diligence activities (oil & gas, power, mining/metals, soft commodities), and nature/biodiversity safeguards (e.g., Ramsar, IUCN I–IV, Arctic projects, non-FSC tropical wood, non-RSPO palm, peatland projects in high-risk geographies).
  - Greenwashing controls: roles/responsibilities clarified, training, product classification committees, ESG classification meetings, and reporting checks.
  - Client engagement and data: sector guidelines, ESG assessments integrated into ratings/approvals, EQAL survey library rollout, Equator Principles for project finance.

- 2024 highlights:
  - New/expanded risk appetite metrics; internal climate model development; finer physical risk granularity in Europe; EPC data/model improvements; advancement of Climate Race integration; biodiversity materiality methodology progress.

- Reporting and disclosures:
  - Regular reporting via Annual Report, ICAAP, Pillar 3; CSRD-aligned disclosures and greenwashing risk mitigation in reporting processes.

- Reputational risk framework:
  - Treated as transition risk; managed via a Group model, governance bodies, transaction structuring reviews, and performance metrics on very high-impact events.

- Financial effects (CSRD E1-9):
  - Methodology outlines scenario/time horizon/location assumptions (RCP 4.5; 2030 non-collateralized, 2050 collateralized; postcode/NUTS3).
  - Exposure sensitive to material physical risk totals EUR 54bn (<3% of total assets), with largest concentration in Europe (44%).

- Nature and biodiversity approach:
  - TNFD LEAP-based portfolio review using ENCORE (dependencies) and UNEP FI Impact Tool (transition impacts).
  - Nature-related heatmap across ESRS E2–E5 topics; no Group-level nature topic deemed material yet; ongoing monitoring.
  - Policy prohibitions and enhanced due diligence to avoid financing in sensitive ecosystems; client annual reviews focus on deforestation risks (e.g., Amazon biome).
  - Nature-based solution initiatives across Brazil, Spain, UK, Mexico; focus on restoration, peatlands, water quality, and reforestation.

- Brazil-focused risk management and impact:
  - Context on deforestation drivers and legal framework; use of satellite monitoring (c. 19,000 properties), embargo/slavery/indigenous land checks, contractual remedies for breaches.
  - Sector protocols and collaborations: Febraban SARB 026/2023 for bovine meat supply chain (traceability, milestones, monitoring and credit actions), RTRS/MBPS, IFACC, NBS Investment Collaborative, Amazon Finance Network.
  - Social development: Jornada Amazônia entrepreneurship platform (training, startups, acceleration, Santander mentoring).

- SAM (Santander Asset Management) perspective:
  - Climate risks (regulatory, technological, market) integrated into ESG analysis to evaluate long-term risk/return, issuer positioning, stranded asset risk, operating costs, and capital access.

- Paris Agreement alignment (net zero 2050):
  - Sectoral targets prioritized for high-emitting, material exposures: power generation, thermal coal, oil & gas, aviation, steel; 2023 addition of auto manufacturing and European auto lending.
  - Methodologies draw on NZBA, PCAF, GFANZ, SBTi; reliance on client data with proxy estimation where needed; acknowledgment of data gaps and reporting lags.
  - Sectors like cement/shipping/aluminium non-material; agriculture, mortgages, CRE monitored; facilitated (capital markets) emissions currently deemed not material.
  - Target-setting sensitive to regulatory, technological, and consumer-behavior dependencies; advocacy for pragmatic, growth-supportive, sector-specific policy pathways given regional divergences and the gap between stated policies and net-zero scenarios.

nodes.title: Aiming to align our activity with the Paris Agreement Goals
nodes.heading: 2.4 Aiming to align our activity with the Paris Agreement Goals
nodes.start_phrase:
In this section we cover how Santander manages the following
IRO:
Adverse impact on climate and the environment due to I-
the bank’s financing of, or investment in, certain non-
sustainable assets and activities.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope
  - Explains Santander’s strategy to align with the Paris Agreement and its net zero by 2050 ambition (announced 2021).
  - Covers how the bank manages climate-related risks and impacts from financed activities, and discloses scopes 1, 2 and 3 (including category 15 financed emissions).

- Methodologies and data
  - Uses NZBA, PCAF, GFANZ, SBTi guidance; external models and datasets; and customer-supplied information.
  - Notes persistent data gaps, regional variability, and time lags; applies proxies and PCAF attribution when needed.

- Sector prioritization and materiality
  - Focuses on high-emitting, material sectors for lending: power generation, oil & gas, aviation, steel, thermal coal, and (from 2023) automotive manufacturing and European auto lending.
  - Sectors like cement, shipping and aluminium deemed not material for now; agriculture, mortgages and commercial real estate (CRE) material on the retail side.
  - Facilitated (capital markets) emissions currently considered not material.

- 2030 alignment targets (wholesale/retail highlights)
  - Power generation: intensity target 0.11 tCO2e/MWh by 2030 (from 0.21 in 2019); portfolio at 0.15 in 2023.
  - Oil & gas: absolute financed emissions target 16.98 MtCO2e by 2030 (−29% vs 2019); portfolio at 20.27 MtCO2e in 2023.
  - Aviation: intensity target 61.71 gCO2e/RPK by 2030 (−33% vs 2019); portfolio at 82.99 in 2023; absolute emissions ~70% below 2019.
  - Steel: intensity target 1.07 tCO2e/t steel by 2030 (−32% vs 2019); portfolio at 1.38 in 2023.
  - Auto manufacturing: intensity target 103 gCO2e/vkm by 2030; portfolio at 134 in 2023.
  - Auto lending Europe: target range 75–89 gCO2e/vkm by 2030 (−35–45% vs 2022); portfolio at 133 in 2023, 2% below target curve.
  - Thermal coal: phase-out by 2030 of exposure to power clients with >10% coal revenues and to thermal coal mining.

- Dependencies and policy stance
  - Emphasizes reliance on regulation, policy clarity, technology progress and consumer behavior; large gap remains between stated policies and net zero pathways (IEA).
  - Advocates for growth-supportive, region-sensitive, predictable transition policies; banks as enablers, not the sole solution.
  - Notes financed emissions may temporarily rise as the bank supports clients’ transition.

- CIB implementation strategy
  - Customer Climate Tiering across four tiers (Leader/Strong/Moderate/Weak) based on two steps: emissions alignment and transition plan quality (Targets, Action plan, Disclosure, Governance).
  - Annual reviews, staff training, and robust data collection; ~three-quarters of in-scope clients held sustainability discussions in 2024.
  - Portfolio steering via quarterly governance and monthly technical reviews; integration into risk appetite, ESCC policy, annual credit reviews, and transaction-level assessments.
  - Collaboration with Oxford’s Transition Finance Centre of Excellence to advance transition finance integrity and tools.

- Sector portfolio insights and evolution
  - Power generation: declining intensity since 2021; mix skewed to project finance; regional differences (Europe leading).
  - Oil & gas: significant drop in financed emissions vs 2021; methodology refined using Wood Mackenzie; energy security remains central.
  - Aviation: exposure reduced; asset-level data adopted; intensity fluctuates with portfolio mix and post-COVID normalization.
  - Steel: small, concentrated portfolio; data improving but gaps remain; intensity ticked up in 2023 after prior decline.
  - Auto manufacturing: stable exposure; continued shift toward EV/PHEV; narrow intensity dispersion across OEMs; JATO data adopted.
  - Auto lending (Europe): actions planned via SCF—OEM partnerships (EV-focused), bundled products (home chargers/solar), EV risk methodologies; success hinges on policy, technology, infrastructure, OEM commitments.
  - Thermal coal: exposure down from €7.0bn (2021) to €4.8bn (2024); transition finance may temporarily lift exposure as clients phase out coal.

- Monitoring of other portfolios (no targets set)
  - Agriculture (Brazil): measures farm-gate scope 1–2 and land-use change; €3.58bn exposure; 9.83 MtCO2e financed emissions; satellite monitoring to prevent financing illegal deforestation; supports low-carbon agriculture, engages in B4ICA; bespoke methodology with WayCarbon and PCAF principles.
  - Spain mortgages and CRE: overcame EPC data gaps via requirements, external databases, and ML estimation; PCAF+CRREM used; 2023 intensities—residential 21.41 kgCO2e/m², CRE 20.02; customer incentives, advisory (CBRE), green credit lines, and renovation financing; alignment depends on PNIEC/ERESSE and EU directives; focus on just transition.
  - UK mortgages and CRE: PCAF framework with CRREM factors; portfolio coverage ~€202bn (mortgages) and €11bn (CRE); 2023 intensities—mortgages 20.87 kgCO2e/m², CRE 25.40; pilots include solar partnership, enhanced EPC advice, cashback, utility partnership product, green mortgages, and retrofit advisory; policy levers include Future Homes Standard and minimum standards.

- Expanding measurement to more portfolios
  - Ongoing efforts to extend financed emissions assessment across Retail and Commercial amid material data gaps (e.g., EPCs in LATAM, SME emissions).

- Asset management (SAM) alignment
  - NZAM signatory; target to halve net emissions by 2030 for 50% of AuM in scope (~27% total AuM); uses NZIF to classify issuer alignment and guide engagement and voting.
  - Participates in Climate Action 100+ and IIGCC Net Zero Engagement Initiative.

- Operational environmental footprint and efficiency
  - Since 2011, scopes 1–2 reduced ~86%; 2024: 96% renewable electricity in 10 core markets; 1,012,554 MWh energy; scope 1: 35,503 tCO2e; scope 2 (market-based): 24,350 tCO2e.
  - 2022–2025 plan invested €38.3m; 69.3 GWh saved; 213.8 GWh converted to renewables; 8,800 kW solar (18.5 GWh output); 37% of workforce in certified buildings; 2,103 EV parking spaces.
  - 2030 Efficiency Plan: on-site renewables/PPAs/RECs; lighting and HVAC upgrades; automated controls; facility modernization; direct emissions cuts (refrigerants, heat pumps, EV fleet); expected additional scope 1–2 reductions; continued offsetting with vetted credits (59,858 in 2024).

- Scope 3 expansions and supply chain
  - Financed emissions (3.15) represent ~99% of scope 3; now also reporting categories 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 3.9; supplier engagement via Aquanima to improve data and reductions.

- Stakeholder engagement and policy advocacy
  - Calls for streamlined, growth-friendly sustainable finance rules, clear sectoral pathways, and recognition of banks’ enabling role.
  - Urges against additional capital requirements tied to ESG risk beyond existing prudential frameworks to avoid hindering transition finance.

nodes.title: Further actions and enablers
nodes.heading: 2.5 Further actions and enablers
nodes.start_phrase: As mentioned previously, we believe that the banks are enablers of the transition and as such, should not be considered as the sole drivers of this process.
nodes.summary:
- Operational decarbonization and offsets
  - Plans to replace conventional boilers with electric heat pumps and deploy renewable energy, self-production, energy efficiency, consumption reduction, and direct emissions reduction measures to cut scope 1 and 2 emissions.
  - Continued offsetting of scope 1 and 2 with carefully vetted, certified carbon credits; in 2024, 59,858 credits were used (85% reduction, 15% removal), validated by an independent rating agency.
  - Waste and awareness: core market offices free of single-use plastics since 2021; “Zero waste” certifications for Santander Group City and Santander España’s central services; ongoing employee environmental awareness campaigns, including Earth Hour participation.

- Scope 3 management
  - Financed emissions (category 3.15) account for ~99% of total scope 3.
  - Expanded reporting to include: 3.1 Purchased goods and services, 3.2 Capital goods, 3.4 Upstream transportation and distribution, 3.9 Downstream transportation and distribution.
  - Supplier engagement (with Aquanima) to obtain vendor carbon footprint data and improve emissions quality and reduction actions.

- Policy advocacy and stakeholder engagement
  - Banks positioned as enablers—not sole drivers—of the net-zero transition; call for coherent, streamlined, and globally aligned regulation.
  - Support for simplifying sustainable finance frameworks to reduce market complexity and regulatory burden; caution against increasing capital requirements linked to ESG risk drivers, which could hinder transition financing, especially in emerging markets.
  - Ongoing engagement with authorities, supervisors, NGOs, and sector bodies to facilitate effective transition finance.

- Partnerships and sector initiatives
  - Participation in: WEF International Business Council (Transforming Energy Demand), WEF Alliance of CEO Climate Leaders, BEI/Bank 2030 (CISL), NZBA (founding member) and NZAM, Financing the Just Transition Alliance (LSE/Grantham), PCAF (financed emissions disclosure), TNFD Forum (including LATAM pilots), and the EU Energy Efficiency Financing Coalition.

- Governance, policies, and controls
  - Board and senior committees (e.g., Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Culture Committee; Audit; Risk committees) oversee the transition plan, portfolio alignment targets, climate finance reporting, and sustainability disclosures.
  - Climate metrics embedded in remuneration: long-term incentives (2024–2026) with 20% sustainability weighting tied to green finance and transition plan delivery.
  - Business integration across CIB, Wealth, Consumer, and local units coordinated by Group Responsible Banking; cross-functional working groups on policy, regulatory monitoring, environmental footprint, and sustainable bonds.
  - ESG Reporting & Internal Control team (since Q2 2023) strengthens data governance, automation, and control of ESG disclosures; emissions targets for scopes 1 & 2 reviewed in the ESG Reporting Forum.
  - Group-wide ESG classification panels (led by Risk) standardize green/social/sustainable labeling; Internal Audit covers climate risk.
  - Key frameworks include the ESCC risk policy and Responsible Banking & Sustainability policy; ongoing climate training and skills development.

- Social information: employees
  - Employee strategy centered on an attractive value proposition, health and well-being, fair/competitive pay, work-life balance, and an inclusive, meritocratic culture.
  - Talent and skills development: continuous learning, role-based development programs, domestic/international mobility, and lifelong learning pathways.
  - Talent attraction in 2024 emphasized digital transformation, graduate internships, and strengthening the EVP; 33,175 new hires.
  - Talent management uses a potential review model (since 2022) to align skills, experience, and aspirations with business needs.
  - Global workforce distributed across Europe, North America, and South America.

nodes.heading: 3.1.1 Talent and skills development
nodes.start_phrase: This section outlines how we manage the following IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from the Sustainability (Social information) section of the 2024 Annual Report, focused on “Supporting employees, communities and customers,” specifically 3.1 Our employees (Talent and skills development; Working conditions).
- People strategy and employee value proposition: Attract and retain talent through growth opportunities, innovative ways of working, inspiring projects, inclusive and meritocratic culture, fair/competitive pay, health and well-being, and flexible work-life balance.
- Workforce definition and footprint: “Employees” are those with active employment contracts at consolidated group entities (excludes interns, suspended contracts, outsourced/self-employed workers, and other value-chain workers). Total workforce around 206,753, with regional distribution: Europe 42.2%, North America 20.0%, South America 37.8%.
- Talent attraction: 33,175 new hires in 2024; emphasis on digital transformation roles, graduate/internship programs, and strengthening the EVP.
- Talent management: Group-wide potential review model (since 2022) covering 124,112 employees to inform personalized development plans; common leadership profile and assessment methodology to foster transformational, collaborative leadership and support strategic decisions and succession.
- International mobility: Global policy approved by the HR Committee/Board to develop talent, strengthen succession, attract external talent, build global mindset, meet business needs, and ensure transparent mobility criteria.
- Learning and development: EUR 64 million invested in 2024. Dojo digital platform accessed by 173,309 employees, offering 174,223 course references with personalized recommendations to promote lifelong learning. Elevate (global learning community) for senior leaders with digital learning paths (People, Tech, Strategy, Change) and peer networks.
- Skills building and certification: Focus on young talent and digital business profiles (e.g., Young Leaders, BeTech & Business). 103,154 employees trained in core business/tech/people/banking skills. 17,305 employees earned independently issued certificates to validate new skills and support career mobility.
- Mandatory and sustainability training: 13 mandatory topics (e.g., sustainability, code of conduct, harassment prevention, cybersecurity, financial crime, data protection), plus local regulatory training. Green Finance training for Retail & Commercial, mandatory ESG integration in commercial processes, Board session on sustainability/ESRS, ESG Talks series, and expanded learning on inclusion, environment, and H&S. Employee rating on learning usefulness/development: 8.7/10 (top 5% of the sector).
- Health, safety, and well-being: General health, safety and well-being policy applied Group-wide in line with local laws. Subsidiaries with >500 employees (covering 99% of the Group) operate OHS systems. Collaboration with public health authorities, employee representatives, and insurers; regular medical checks and return-to-work assessments.
- Risk prevention and safe workplaces: OHS plans reviewed with employee councils; periodic risk assessments; prevention-by-design in spaces/tools; safe-work procedures and certifications; emergency/evacuation and first-aid training; posture/ergonomics measures; accident investigations; active H&S committees with employee delegates.
- BeHealthy program: In its 8th year, built on four pillars (know your numbers, eat well, move, be balanced). >64,000 employees participated in 2024, including BeHealthy Week and WHO-linked events. Offerings include mental health and emotional support, sports and nutrition apps, preventive care, and discounted health services. Employee ratings: 8.4/10 that health/well-being is a priority (top 25% of sector) and 8.4/10 for physical/mental well-being support.
- Work-life balance: Flexible work options; paid paternity/adoption and caregiver leave across all entities.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities addressed: 
  - I+: Promote continuous career development; safeguard health, safety, and well-being; ensure fair, market-aligned remuneration under equal, merit-based conditions; enable flexible work.
  - I-: Avoid harm through discrimination, inadequate conditions, harassment, or corruption.
  - R: Manage potential conflict with employees from infringement of rights.

nodes.title: Working conditions
nodes.heading: 3.1.2 Working conditions
nodes.start_phrase: This section outlines how we manage these IROs:
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Extract from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability) covering Working Conditions (health, safety, well-being, work-life balance, social protection, labor rights, data protection), Remuneration and Benefits, and Inclusive Culture, with governance oversight and measurable outcomes.
- Managing impacts/risks/opportunities (IROs):
  - Promote employee health, safety, security, inclusion and flexible work-life balance.
  - Prevent harm from discrimination, poor conditions, harassment or corruption.
  - Ensure fair, market-based, merit-driven pay and benefits.
  - Mitigate risks of labor-rights conflicts through dialogue and compliance.
- Employee health, safety and well-being:
  - Group-wide systems and policies aligned with local laws; sector collective agreements include occupational risk prevention.
  - 99% of the Group (subsidiaries >500 employees) covered by OH&S systems; regular medical check-ups; coordination with authorities and insurers.
  - Prevention measures: risk assessments, safe-by-design workspaces/tools, quality/safety procedures and certifications, emergency/evacuation and first aid, ergonomic/postural risk mitigation, accident investigations, active H&S committees.
  - BeHealthy program (8th year): >64,000 participants; global events (BeHealthy Week, WHO campaigns). Access to mental health/emotional support, fitness, nutrition and prevention services.
  - Employee survey ratings: 8.4/10 “health & well-being is a priority”; 8.4/10 “support for physical/mental well-being.”
- Work-life balance and flexibility:
  - Paid parental/adoption and family care leave in all entities; 2024: 8,195 parental/adoption leaves; 2,824 family care leaves (total 10,874; 5.3% of workforce; 6.7% women; 3.7% men).
  - Broad flexi-working in central services across nine core markets (remote work and flexible hours), continually reviewed for productivity and customer needs.
  - Flexibility rating: 8.8/10.
- Social protection and employment conditions:
  - Income protection for sickness/disability per local law; additional private cover in core markets; typically full pay during sickness.
  - 98% permanent contracts; unemployment coverage per local laws.
  - Occupational accident pay protection; supplements in some countries (e.g., Spain).
  - Group minimum standard for paid parental leave: 14–30 weeks fully paid for primary caregivers; 4 weeks fully paid for secondary caregivers; 76% of new mothers remain employed 12 months after returning.
  - Retirement coverage via public/private schemes; defined contribution plans in core markets.
- Collective bargaining and social dialogue:
  - Commitment to freedom of association and collective bargaining; alignment with ILO Fundamental Conventions and Group policies.
  - 110,692 employees in locations with union representation; active European Business Council; ongoing bilateral and committee engagements.
  - 2024 agreements in core countries on OH&S, gender-balance monitoring, pension oversight, training, and CBA updates.
  - Brazil: preventive measures and provisions for common labor claims; oversight committee; digitized departure records; strengthened working-hours registration in line with jurisprudence.
- Employee data protection:
  - Processing under labor and data protection laws with Group procedures, tools and controls; cross-reference to privacy, data protection and cybersecurity section.
- Remuneration and corporate benefits:
  - Pay framework blends fixed and variable compensation tied to Group/individual performance, behaviors, risk and sustainability; non-discriminatory and market-aligned; dignified pay.
  - All employees paid at or above legal minimum; 99% receive additional remuneration (benefits, pensions, incentives, variable pay).
  - Variable schemes across all businesses reward meritocracy and team/individual contributions; executive directors’ variable pay includes sustainability (8%) and climate (2%) goals.

nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Customer conduct, consumer protection, and financial inclusion in Santander’s 2024 Annual Report (sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2).
- Customer conduct risk and IROs: Identifies risks of losses and customer harm from inadequate practices, insufficient information, and poor complaints access; sets opportunities to improve outcomes.
- Customer conduct risk model: Approved by the compliance and conduct committee; aligns with the “Simple, Personal and Fair” culture; covers product/service design, sales, and post‑sales; emphasizes fair treatment, transparency, responsible sales/pricing, data protection, complaints handling, financial education, fraud safeguards, and attention to vulnerable customers/overindebtedness.
- Governance: Product governance and consumer protection within Compliance oversees execution; Board supervises product approval and remuneration policies; remuneration and risk committees and compliance forums set risk appetite and monitor conduct risk.
- Policies, guides, and accessibility: Group-wide policies ensure consistent implementation and communication; 2024 focus on the European Accessibility Directive to improve access to products, services, and channels, with tech and UX enhancements.
- Monitoring and metrics: Risk appetite metrics for claims/internal events to detect and manage issues; 2024 dispute impacts noted (mortgage fees in Spain, CHF mortgages in Poland) with appropriate customer responses.
- Product/service approval: Formal policy mandates transparent, fair, needs‑based design and pricing; local and corporate forums require unanimous approval and use standardized documentation and reviews across the lifecycle and channels.
- Conduct training and licensing: Mandatory refresher training for all employees; adherence to regulatory certifications (e.g., MiFID) and specialized training for sales teams.
- Pay linked to conduct: At least 40% of sales variable pay tied to quality and conduct metrics to reinforce good customer outcomes and target‑market suitability.
- Sales monitoring: Ongoing lifecycle oversight using Customer Voice (queries, complaints, surveys) and sales controls (e.g., early cancellations) to trigger improvements; 2024 actions included stronger welcome communications, call‑center sales enhancements in Mexico, and tighter campaign governance in Poland.
- Post‑sales fraud conduct: 2024 integration of conduct guidelines into the Group Fraud Policy; 2024–2026 improvement plans to unify fraud case channels, standardize taxonomies, enhance communications, and strengthen first/second line controls, with special focus on vulnerable customers; additional controls via NPS and QA.
- Complaints handling: Multi‑channel access and escalation options (e.g., Ombudsman/regulators); digital investments to speed resolution and enable self‑service; structured root‑cause analysis with action plans and senior oversight; 2024 progress across all countries, including a 19% claims reduction in Spain (ex‑sector events).
- AI in complaints: Global working group to enhance platforms; AI embedded in registration/analysis. Brazil’s “Viva Voz” scaled analysis from 3% in two days to 60% in one day (aiming 100%); Spain and Poland piloting similar tools.
- Complaint profile and outcomes: Standardized Group metrics show distribution by type (e.g., banking procedures, loans, investments, payments, insurance, others) and resolution rates, with the majority resolved in favour of the bank.
- Vulnerable customers: Group regulations (Nov 2023) on vulnerability and overindebtedness rolled out in 2024 to unify standards; indicators and a methodology under development to identify and address vulnerabilities proactively; bi‑monthly global‑local coordination and global staff training launched.
- Financial inclusion and health (3.3.2): Strategic priority to support social progress, prosperity, and entrepreneurship with tailored solutions in each market.
- Measurement approach: Uses World Bank Global Findex to size unbanked/underbanked/financially distressed populations; considers access, use, and financing; assesses involuntary exclusion via perceived barriers; applies a correction factor reflecting Santander’s market penetration to gauge addressable inclusion needs.

- Context: Excerpts from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report covering customer conduct, financial inclusion and health, vulnerable customer management, complaints handling, and the start of privacy/data protection and cybersecurity.
- Customer complaints: Standardized claims metric used group-wide; breakdown of complaint types (e.g., banking procedures, loans, investments, payment methods, insurance, others) and resolution outcomes (in favour of the bank vs. customer).
- Vulnerable customers: Group regulations on vulnerable customers and prevention of over-indebtedness approved in Nov 2023 and embedded across markets in 2024. Use of indicators and a developing methodology to identify potential vulnerability and adapt services. Bi‑monthly coordination between local units and global team; global employee training rolled out.
- Financial inclusion strategy and measurement: Inclusion and financial health positioned as drivers of social progress. Market sizing of unbanked, underbanked, and financially distressed segments using World Bank Global Findex, with definitions and an adjustment for Santander’s market penetration.
- Inclusion target and progress: Ambition to reach 5 million people with inclusion measures in 2023–2025; cumulative progress shown (about 1.8 million in 2023 and 4.3 million by 2024). In 2024, roughly 1.0 million included via access initiatives and 1.6 million via finance initiatives.
- Access initiatives: Expanding access to cash and transactions via remote/underserved-area branches and third‑party partnerships (e.g., Correos Cash in Spain; retailers like Oxxo/7‑Eleven in Mexico; mobile/remote solutions in Portugal, Argentina, Poland, Uruguay). Promoting digital access (wallets, POS, programs like Cashless Poland and Chile’s Mas Lucas), basic accounts beyond regulatory minimums, and tailored support for seniors. Getnet enhances digital payments access for underbanked merchants and individuals.
- Finance initiatives: Microfinance in Latin America since 2002 supporting low-income and underbanked entrepreneurs—evolving from microcredit to broader microfinance (basic accounts, financial education, microinsurance). Efficiency gains via technology (mobile branches, faster disbursement). Mixed group/individual lending models adapted by country (greater individual lending in Peru and Colombia; growing in Brazil and Mexico).
- Additional finance-based support: Debt relief and hardship programs (e.g., Portugal’s Iris; UK tools and assistance; Spain mortgage relief). Affordable housing initiatives (Spain’s Social Housing Fund, affordable rentals; US LMI housing support). Targeted credit for groups with constrained access (SMEs at risk limits in Spain, LMI small businesses in the US, limited-credit-history entrepreneurs in Argentina, special programs in Mexico).
- Financial health: Defined as the ability to manage short-term needs and long-term goals to avoid distress. Initiatives include money-management tools, debt calculators, advisory, and financial education to complement inclusion. 2024 saw metrics set to monitor financial health, particularly for over-indebted customers.
- Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity: Introduction of IROs related to personal data protection, cybersecurity awareness, and potential regulatory and reputational risks. Emphasis on compliance with data protection laws and Group standards amid increased data processing from digitalization.

nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from Banco Santander’s Annual Report 2024, Governance – Business Conduct (Section 4), covering corporate culture and ethical conduct, including conduct standards and responsible taxation.

- 4.1 Corporate culture – The Santander Way:
  - Culture foundations: values (Simple, Personal, Fair), corporate behaviours (TEAMS), leadership principles (Group first, lead transformation, grow talent, display TEAMS, drive inclusion), and a strong risk culture (Risk Pro).
  - 2024 actions: embedded behaviours and leadership principles in talent processes; boosted employee upskilling aligned to business needs; evolved Dojo digital learning platform for personalized, role‑based, continuous learning; used the YourVoice listening program to shape action plans; reinforced culture through MyContribution performance review (50% what, 40% how, 10% risk management).
  - Governance: Global Culture Policy sets common standards across all subsidiaries.

- 4.2 Ethical conduct – scope of risks and responsibilities:
  - Focus on acting responsibly toward investors, employees, society and the environment; paying taxes to support wealth distribution; preventing bribery/corruption and financial crime (e.g., AML).

- 4.2.1 Conduct standards – General Code of Conduct (GCC):
  - GCC approved by the Board; applies to all employees, management, and subsidiaries; publicly available.
  - Promotes equal opportunity, non‑discrimination, zero tolerance for harassment, respect, work‑life balance, human rights, and environmental protection.
  - Implementation:
    - Mandatory annual training (including penal responsibility, conflicts of interest, gifts/invitations), with an employee pledge.
    - #YourConductMatters awareness campaigns; guidance from Compliance; Canal Abierto whistleblowing channel; breaches sanctioned per regulation.
  - Monitoring and outcomes: GCC training completion tracked as a risk appetite metric; 99.1% completion as of Dec 2024; mandatory training tied to performance reviews; incidents linked to GCC violations are monitored.
  - Policy alignment: Conflicts of Interest Policy updated and simplified; Procurement Management Conduct Policy integrated.

- 4.2.2 Responsible taxation:
  - Tax strategy aligned with purpose and business strategy; Board approval and periodic review; risk management through the internal control model.
  - Cooperative compliance: adheres to Spain’s and the UK’s tax practice codes (since 2010), Portugal’s (since 2022), and submits an annual Tax Transparency Report to Spain’s Tax Authority (since 2015).
  - Core principles: comply with tax obligations per the spirit and intention of the law; respect transfer pricing and pay taxes per operations, risks and profits in each jurisdiction; do not provide tax advice or planning strategies when marketing/selling financial products.

nodes.summary:
- Scope of the excerpt: Sustainability governance on ethical conduct, responsible taxation, financial-crime compliance, and ethical reporting channels within Grupo Santander’s 2024 Annual Report.

- Ethical conduct and conduct standards (GCC):
  - Group-wide General Code of Conduct approved by the Board; applies to all employees, management and subsidiary governing bodies; published on the corporate website.
  - Core values: equal opportunity, non-discrimination, zero tolerance of harassment, respect, work-life balance, human rights, and environmental protection.
  - Implementation mechanisms: mandatory annual GCC training and employee pledge; #YourConductMatters awareness campaigns; Compliance function for queries; Canal Abierto whistleblowing channel; breaches sanctioned per regulation.
  - Risk management: quarterly tracking of mandatory training completion as a risk appetite metric (99.1% completion as of Dec-2024; no remediation required); training tied to performance reviews; monitoring incidents linked to GCC violations.

- Responsible taxation:
  - Board-approved tax strategy aligned with purpose and sustainable, responsible banking; governed by an internal control-based tax risk management model.
  - Cooperative compliance: adheres to Spanish and UK codes since 2010, Portuguese code since 2022; voluntary Tax Transparency Report to Spain’s Tax Authority since 2015.
  - Principles: comply with the spirit and intent of tax law; arm’s-length transfer pricing aligned to value creation, risks and profits; do not market tax advice/planning or facilitate customer tax avoidance; transparent country-by-country disclosure; restrictions on non-cooperative jurisdictions require Board approval and enhanced oversight.
  - 2024 tax contribution: EUR 22.5bn total taxes; EUR 10.9bn paid directly (includes EUR 5.9bn income tax paid; 30.9% effective rate on cash taxes); income tax expense EUR 5.3bn (27.8% effective rate), with timing differences explained.

- Financial crime compliance (FCC):
  - Board-approved corporate FCC framework covering AML/CFT, sanctions, and since 2023 anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABC); policies and CDD/KYC aligned to domestic/international rules and updated for evolving threats.
  - Centralized oversight with technical FCC units; extensive awareness via training, intranet, campaigns, and newsletters; continuous engagement with businesses to identify and mitigate new risks.
  - Inclusion with control: unbiased FCC onboarding for “people in special situations” with appropriate due diligence; flexible remote/in-person onboarding.
  - Sector risk approach: enhanced KYC and transaction monitoring for sectors with elevated risks (corruption, trafficking, modern slavery, labor exploitation, child abuse, environmental crime).
  - ABC program: group-wide RCSA; higher exposure areas include Marketing, Sponsorships, Vendor Management, and HR; tailored training including procurement teams and board members; 166,199 employees trained in FCC; strengthened outsourcing/supplier controls with greater automation.
  - Detection and reporting: robust FIU-led systems, internal controls, and independent investigation committees; 2024 outcomes—453,175 investigations and 231,810 disclosures to authorities; FCC-related concerns can also be raised via whistleblowing channels.
  - No finalized judicial or administrative proceedings in 2024 related to corruption/anti-bribery or AML/CFT, per stated materiality criteria.

- Ethical channels (Canal Abierto):
  - Anonymous, confidential whistleblowing channel with anti-retaliation protections; local channels per subsidiary in multiple languages under common standards since 2020.
  - Minimum standards: CEO endorsement, employee communication and lessons learned, easy access and anonymity, external reporting platforms, conflict-of-interest safeguards in investigations, and regular internal audits.
  - Governance: Board-approved policy and operating procedure; Banco Santander’s channel overseen by the Chief Compliance Officer; accessible via intranet and corporate website.
  - Scope: primarily for employees; some subsidiaries open to vendors/customers; excludes standard business incidents/complaints.
  - Reportable matters include GCC breaches, unlawful acts, SOX-related issues, AML/CFT and ABC breaches, securities law violations, serious legal/administrative offenses, and conduct against corporate behaviors.
  - Case handling: diligent, independent, objective processing; typical 60-day timeline extendable by 30 days; explicit conflict-of-interest management; prohibition of reprisals.
  - Culture and oversight: GCC training includes Canal Abierto module; ongoing awareness communications; annual consolidated reporting to the Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee and the Audit Committee; continuous improvement focus on analytics to inform governing bodies and action plans.

nodes.title: Ethical channels
nodes.heading: 4.3 Ethical channels
nodes.start_phrase: In this section we cover how Santander manages these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Ethical channels (whistleblowing) and supplier responsibility within Santander’s Sustainability, Governance, Risk and Compliance framework.
- Ethical reporting channel (Canal Abierto):
  - Anonymous, confidential Group-wide channel to report unethical conduct; anti-retaliation explicitly enforced.
  - Local implementations across Group units in multiple languages, aligned to a 2020 Group policy with minimum standards (CEO endorsement, accessibility and anonymity, external platforms, conflict-of-interest controls, regular internal audits).
  - Governance: Board-approved policy; Banco Santander channel under the Chief Compliance Officer; procedures published on corporate site and platform.
  - Scope and use: Accessible via intranet for employees and via corporate website/platform for stakeholders; some local channels open to vendors and customers; business complaints outside scope are excluded.
  - Reportable matters include: unlawful acts; breaches of the General Code of Conduct (GCC); accounting/audit irregularities (SOX); AML/CFT, corruption and bribery; securities law violations; serious legal/administrative/EU-law infringements; conduct contrary to corporate behaviours.
  - Case handling commitments: diligent, independent, objective investigations; 60-day processing target (+30 days for complex cases); conflict-of-interest management; strict anti-retaliation.
  - Awareness and oversight: mandatory annual Code of Conduct training including Canal Abierto; ongoing communications with statistics and guidance; annual consolidated reporting by Compliance to the Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee and the Audit Committee.
  - Monitoring and assurance: quarterly data collection on volumes, types, and measures; regular external auditor review of data integrity and traceability.
- 2024 Canal Abierto outcomes:
  - 4,437 reports received (2.1% of headcount), including 216 from third parties (163 customers, 53 vendors); increase from 3,611 in 2023 due to a wider business perimeter.
  - Categories (selected counts): GCC breaches 2,286; marketing 321; privacy/security/confidentiality 116; internal fraud 292; harassment 1,094 (per CSRD definition; 89% workplace harassment); equal opportunities/non-discrimination 132; conflicts of interest 219; other GCC 112; HR cases 1,754; other typologies 397.
  - Closed reports: 4,122; disciplinary actions: 715, including 393 dismissals (0.2% of headcount).
  - Corruption-specific: 14 reports led to 3 dismissals.
  - No judicial proceedings recorded for discrimination or violations of fundamental rights; no employee cases referring to serious human rights incidents.
  - Data scope: multiple countries and Group units (e.g., Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Spain, Mexico, Poland, Portugal, UK, US, etc., including Digital Consumer Bank subsidiaries and SCIB branches).
- Supplier responsibility and ESG in procurement:
  - Objectives (IROs): promote responsible practices with vendors, assess ESG performance, provide improvement tools; mitigate risks to operational resilience by vetting supplier solvency, reputation, and legal compliance.
  - Group-wide outsourcing and third‑party management model plus third‑party certification policy to ensure minimum standards and manage risks in resilience, solvency, reputation, and regulatory compliance.
  - Supplier ESG certification methodology to identify higher sustainability risk suppliers and calibrate controls accordingly, complementing the third‑party certification policy.
  - Capacity building: support suppliers via the UN Global Compact training programme to enhance sustainability knowledge and implementation.
  - 2024 progress: began embedding a new ESG approval methodology across the Group to strengthen sustainability in procurement.

nodes.title: Our suppliers
nodes.heading: 4.4 Our suppliers
nodes.start_phrase: In this section we cover how Santander manages these IRO:
nodes.summary:
- Ethics and whistleblowing: Quarterly monitoring and external audit of ethical channel data. In 2024, 4,437 reports were received (2.1% of headcount), including 216 from third parties; 4,122 were closed, leading to 715 disciplinary actions and 393 dismissals (0.2% of headcount). Main categories included breaches to the Group Code of Conduct, harassment (defined per CSRD; 89% workplace harassment), internal fraud, equal opportunities/non-discrimination, conflicts of interest, privacy/security, and other compliance areas (incl. AML/CTF, corruption and bribery—14 corruption reports, 3 dismissals). Increase vs. 2023 (3,611) reflects a broader perimeter. The Group reports no judicial proceedings for discrimination/fundamental rights and no serious human rights incidents involving employees.

- Supplier management and ESG: Group-wide outsourcing/third‑party certification and an ESG certification methodology to identify and control sustainability risks; support via UN Global Compact training. A new ESG approval methodology pre‑classifies suppliers by sector exposure (S&P ESG Risk Atlas) and assigns low/medium/high risk using surveys (country risk, size, environmental traits). By year‑end, 487 at‑risk suppliers were assessed; remediation plans applied as needed. Sustainability criteria are embedded in procurement (e.g., cards, electricity, vehicles) and requested in tenders with high ESG impact (ATMs, hardware, cash transport), covering carbon footprint, recycled materials, energy efficiency, accessibility, and legal compliance. A corporate tool standardizes high‑risk supplier certification and reviews risks (cybersecurity, continuity, data protection, anti‑bribery, etc.). Ethical channels for suppliers are being expanded; expert teams are being built.

- Supplier payments: EUR 11.6bn paid; 89% local suppliers (88% of volume). Average payment 15 days; 81% within legal maximum; implementing SME‑specific controls. No significant term differences and no judicial/administrative proceedings for non‑payment.

- Sustainability statement basis and scope: The report is Santander Group’s consolidated non‑financial and sustainability information under EU CSRD (Directive 2022/2464) and related regulation, aligned with Spanish law; approved 25 Feb 2024; covers 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024. Topic scopes are specified: climate/transition (CIB portfolios in thermal coal, power, O&G, aviation, steel, autos; DCB auto loans; Brazil agro; Spain/UK mortgages and real estate), Equator Principles (CIB), environmental footprint (Group-wide with defined Scope 3 exceptions), EU Taxonomy GAR (prudential group), and employee metrics (Group scope with noted exclusions).
