structure.title: Introduction, basis of presentation of the Sustainability statement and other information
structure.heading: SN 1. Introduction, basis of presentation of the Sustainability statement and other information
structure.start_phrase: 2013/34/EU as regards disclosure of non-financial and diversity information.
structure.summary:
- Nature and regulatory basis of the statement: Consolidated non‑financial and sustainability information for Banco Santander, S.A. and subsidiaries, approved by the board on 25 February 2024. Prepared in line with CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (ESRS), Spanish Commercial Code Art. 49 (Act 11/2018 transposing Directive 2014/95/EU), and EU Taxonomy (Reg. (EU) 2021/2178). Reporting period: 1 January–31 December 2024; same consolidated basis as the financial statements with defined scope differences by topic.

- Scope overview by topic (examples):
  - Environmental: Green finance (CIB), EV financing (Digital Consumer Bank), cards in sustainable materials (main Group companies across multiple countries), ESG in risk management (Group), portfolio exposure to climate‑sensitive sectors (Group), Equator Principles (CIB), climate alignment for specified sectoral portfolios and geographies, environmental footprint (Group with defined Scope 3 coverage), EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (prudential group).
  - Social: Employees (headcount, remuneration, training, engagement; Group scope with noted exceptions), communities (SRI AuMs in Wealth; education/employability support across main geographies and foundations; other community programmes across Group markets), customers (coverage of customer base/offices/channels; NPS in main geographies; complaints for entities >1% of claims; financial health & inclusion across major markets).
  - Governance: Corporate governance and shareholder/investor communications (Banco Santander, S.A.), ethical conduct (mandatory GCC training), tax contribution (Group), financial crime compliance (main obliged entities), litigation and penalties (Group), ethical channels across multiple geographies, supplier management (payments and ESG‑risk‑evaluated suppliers across specified countries).

- Subsidiary reporting under CSRD: Within the consolidation perimeter, Santander Consumer Bank AS (Norway), Santander Bank Polska S.A. (Poland), and Stellantis Banque France (France) are obliged to report. Entities in countries where CSRD is not yet transposed are not considered obliged. No exemption used for information on upcoming events/negotiations. No additional significant post‑period events (from 1 January 2025 to report preparation) beyond those in the annual accounts.

- Value chain definition and coverage: Constructed per ESRS 1 and EFRAG guidance; split into upstream (financial authorities, product/service providers), own operations (assets, geographies, cross‑cutting functions), and downstream (Retail & Commercial Banking; Digital Consumer Bank including Openbank and SCF; CIB; Wealth Management & Insurance; Payments via PagoNxt and Cards; JVs/associates; retailers such as car dealerships).

- Information not disclosed: Partial disclosure of ESRS 2 MDR‑A (OpEx/CapEx for action plans) due to confidentiality/sensitivity; selected spend metrics provided (e.g., training, energy efficiency, community investment). No other exclusions for IP/know‑how.

- Time horizons used: Short term 1 year; medium term 1–5 years; long term >5 years, aligned with ESRS and explicitly indicated where different.

- Significant estimates and assumptions: Heavy reliance on third‑party data and estimates for GHG emissions, climate target‑setting and forward‑looking parameters; subject to methodological, data, market, technological, and regulatory uncertainties. Expect improvements in data quality/coverage; Group may update targets and methodologies. EU Taxonomy disclosures also subject to data uncertainty.

- Comparatives and methodological changes:
  - Transitional provision used under ESRS 1: no prior‑year comparatives in first year, except where required by Spanish Law 11/2018.
  - Method changes: calendar days lost now include fatalities; energy consumption recalculated by country generation mix and certified renewable electricity; Scope 1 now includes refrigerant gas leaks.
  - Scope changes: internal consumption now covers 100% of Group; compensation of Scopes 1 and 2 now for 100% of Group from 2024.
  - Scope 1 and 2 reduction targets reviewed (2020 baseline, 2030 horizon). No material restatements identified.

- Incorporation by reference: Specific ESRS requirements are fulfilled via cross‑references to the consolidated annual accounts and audit report (e.g., subsidiary list; penalties; linkage of OpEx/CapEx to accounts; tax information; serious human rights incidents for employees/affected groups/consumers; anti‑corruption/bribery fines). A CSRD content index (SN 11) maps requirements to report sections.

- ESRS phase‑in provisions applied (not disclosed in year one): 
  - ESRS 2 SBM‑1 (total revenue/revenue by significant ESRS sectors)
  - ESRS 2 SBM‑3 (potential financial effects)
  - ESRS E1‑9 (potential physical/transition risks and climate opportunities)
  - ESRS S1‑7 (non‑employee worker characteristics)
  - ESRS S1‑14 (H&S for non‑employee workers)
  - ESRS S1‑15 (work‑life balance)

- Cross‑references to datapoints from other EU legislation and their materiality/location: Includes board diversity and independence (Delegated Reg. 2020/1816), due diligence statement, involvement in fossil fuels/chemicals/controversial weapons/tobacco (with some deemed not material), and E1‑1 transition plan and Paris‑aligned benchmark considerations; mapped to relevant Sustainability Notes and sections.

structure.title: Sustainability governance
structure.heading: SN 2. Sustainability governance
structure.summary:
- Presents a comprehensive cross-reference of ESRS 2 and topical ESRS datapoints that derive from other EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3 Article 449a, EU Climate Law, EU Benchmark Regulations), indicating for each datapoint whether it is material and where it appears in the report (e.g., sections and Sustainability Notes).
- Climate (ESRS E1) disclosures highlighted as material include: transition plan to climate neutrality by 2050; Paris-alignment/transition alignment metrics; GHG emissions reduction targets; energy consumption and mix; energy intensity in high-impact sectors; gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions and intensity; GHG removals and carbon credits; portfolio exposure to climate-related physical risks, including disaggregation by acute/chronic risks, location of significant assets at risk, and real estate energy-efficiency classes; degree of exposure to climate-related opportunities (some items phased in). These link to CRR/Pillar 3 templates and EU Delegated/Implementing Regulations and are located mainly in “Our climate transition plan” and Sustainability Notes (SN 4, SN 7.1).
- Other environmental topics (ESRS E2–E5) are largely deemed not material for the period: pollutants to air/water/soil (E2-4), water and marine resources policies and metrics (E3-1, E3-4), biodiversity and ecosystems (E4-2 incl. oceans/seas and deforestation policies), waste (E5-5, incl. hazardous/radioactive waste).
- Social standards: Employees (ESRS S1) include human rights policy commitments and due diligence (ILO core conventions), workplace accident prevention systems, grievance mechanisms, fatalities/accident days lost, unadjusted gender pay gap, CEO pay ratio, and incidents of discrimination; some datapoints (e.g., trafficking prevention) are not material. Value chain workers (S2), affected communities (S3), and consumers/end-users (S4) are mostly not material, with cross-references to customer and human rights sections where relevant.
- Governance (ESRS G1): anti-corruption and anti-bribery standards, fines, and whistleblower protection are disclosed and linked to Business Conduct and Financial Crime Compliance.
- Governance structure and oversight:
  - Board of Directors: 15 members (13 non-executive, 2 executive), 66.67% independent; gender split 40% women/60% men (reported diversity ratio 67%); broad international background; explicit responsibility for responsible banking and sustainability strategy, KPIs, and oversight.
  - Responsible Banking, Sustainability and Culture Committee (RBSCC): 5 independent directors (80% women); advises on strategy/policies for E, S, G; 2024 agenda included climate strategy/targets, ESG in credit process, green finance, own footprint and value-chain emissions, social agenda (financial inclusion, human rights), community support/Universidades, inclusive culture and women in senior roles, embedding sustainability in remuneration, supplier ESG, non-financial reporting, regulatory trends, and CSRD training.
  - Audit Committee: 5 independent directors (60% women); oversees financial and sustainability reporting processes and internal controls; 15 meetings in 2024, including joint sessions with the risk committee.
  - Risk Supervision, Regulation and Compliance Committee: 5 external directors (40% women; 3 independent); oversees financial and non-financial risks, risk appetite, culture; 18 meetings in 2024; topics included data protection, operational resilience, conduct, complaints and whistleblowing.
  - Nomination and Remuneration Committees also review sustainability-related issues (e.g., integration of sustainability targets into remuneration).
- Management committees and three lines of defence:
  - Corporate Accounting and Financial Reporting, Management and Sustainability Committee approves and validates sustainability disclosures; meets monthly.
  - Risk Control Committee offers a holistic risk view against risk appetite.
  - First line (business/functions) owns and manages risks and data for sustainability metrics; Corporate Sustainability leads strategy and coordination; Accounting and Management Control maintains internal control over sustainability information.
  - Second line (Risk; Compliance & Conduct) challenges and oversees risk management and control effectiveness.
  - Third line (Internal Audit) independently assesses adequacy and effectiveness of controls over financial and sustainability reporting and compliance with codes/policies; reports to the Audit Committee.
- Internal control over sustainability information:
  - COSO-based system evolving to cover all material topics; identifies material risks, sets controls, and addresses key challenges (assumptions/judgments, completeness/boundaries, third‑party/value-chain data, consolidation of metrics).
  - Steps toward reasonable assurance for selected sustainability metrics.
  - Control architecture outlined across control culture, risk assessment (RCSA), control activities, information/communication, and monitoring.
- Cross-cutting frameworks and policies embedding ESG:
  - Responsible Banking framework and policy; Accounting & Financial Reporting, Management and Sustainability information framework; Responsible Banking model (roles and responsibilities across the three lines).

structure.title: Materiality assessment – Detailed methodology
structure.heading: SN 3. Materiality assessment – Detailed methodology
structure.start_phrase: The Group and subsidiaries’ double materiality assessments are based on European Sustainability Regulatory Standards (ESRS) 1 and 2, and the Double Materiality Assessment Guide from the ERAG.
structure.summary:
- Overview: Extract from a sustainability and governance section of an annual report detailing the Group’s responsible banking framework, double materiality assessment methodology and results, key impacts/risks/opportunities (IROs) across ESRS topics, and the climate transition plan including financed emissions and target-setting.
- Governance and policy framework: Describes the Responsible Banking and Sustainability Policy (principles, targets incl. human rights), and the Responsible Banking Model (first/second/third lines of defence) to embed ESG. Confirms rigorous drafting/approval/monitoring standards, with approval by the Board or its committees. Lists core corporate frameworks (Responsible Banking, Risk, Cybersecurity, Compliance and Conduct, Financial Crime, HR) and policies (Code of Conduct, Securities Markets Code, Environmental/Social/Climate Risk, Tax, Conflicts of Interest, Defence sector, AML/CFT, Remuneration, Performance, Succession, Culture). Refers to website for full regulatory documents.
- Topical coverage: Signals specific regulations and management approaches for material topics and IROs: climate change, own workforce, customers/consumers, affected communities, and business conduct.
- Double materiality methodology (ESRS 1 and 2; EFRAG guidance): 
  - Phase 1 Background and stakeholder analysis using internal strategic/financial materials plus external sources (UNEP FI impact tool, ENCORE for environmental dependencies, human rights due diligence).
  - Stakeholder mapping and inputs from customers, employees, investors, regulators, NGOs, communities.
  - Phase 2 Identification: 100+ IROs categorized per ESRS AR 16, mapped to value chain, time horizons, dependencies between impacts and risks/opportunities, managerial ownership, and financial effect type.
  - Phase 3 Assessment: 32 IROs deemed material. Impacts assessed on scale, scope, irreparability, and likelihood. Risks assessed via climate risk quantification (transition/physical) aligned with EBA ESG risk guidance; other environmental risks linked to nature/biodiversity approach (ENCORE; Kunming-Montreal GBF target 15); social/governance via SASB and internal financials. Opportunities sized via projected ESG revenues vs Group revenue.
  - Phase 4 Thresholds: Materiality threshold set at 3.5/5 for impact and financial materiality; statistical rationale provided.
- Stakeholder priorities: Broad consensus on prioritizing climate action/green transition, data protection, transparency, and financial inclusion. Retail customers emphasize privacy/transparency; employees/senior management weight ESG areas evenly; investors/regulators/NGOs prioritize environmental issues. Input volumes: 9,000+ retail customers; c.200 employees; 8 investors; 8 senior managers; 3 NGOs; 2 regulators/supervisors.
- IRO register examples (linked to ESRS, value chain, time horizon, and management sections):
  - Climate (E1): Positive impacts from financing renewables/low-carbon tech and reducing own Scope 1–2; negative impacts from financing non-sustainable activities; opportunities for revenue growth across clean tech and sectoral solutions; reputational risk if climate policies/objectives are perceived as inadequate.
  - Own workforce (S1): Positive impacts via health, safety, well-being, flexible work; diversity and equal opportunity; learning and talent development; fair/market-based remuneration. Negative impacts/risks from discrimination, inadequate conditions, misconduct or conflict.
  - Consumers and end users (S4): Positive impacts via inclusive, needs-based products and financial health initiatives; cybersecurity education. Negative impacts/risks from poor disclosure, weak complaints handling, data protection breaches, inadequate treatment of vulnerable customers, and substandard conduct.
  - Affected communities (S3): Positive impacts from education, employability, entrepreneurship programs; lending to support economic growth; socially responsible investment/lending. Negative impacts from financing that breaches ESG policies or insufficient stakeholder due diligence in financing.
  - Business conduct (G1): Positive impacts from ethical culture, tax contribution, effective whistleblowing channels, responsible supply chain management. Negative impacts/risks from corruption/bribery, ineffective grievance processes, vendor solvency/reputation/compliance weaknesses, and financial crime.
- Climate transition plan (SN 4):
  - Target design: Uses physical emissions intensity for power generation, steel, aviation, auto manufacturing; absolute emissions for oil & gas. Emphasizes engagement over divestment and case-by-case judgment to avoid perverse incentives; acknowledges lack of a universal “transition finance taxonomy.”
  - Scenario basis: 2030 alignment targets anchored in IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (IEA-NZE), consistent with a 1.5°C pathway; own Scope 1–2 reduction aligned with SBTi cross-sector absolute reduction (>4.2% linear annual).
  - Coverage and baselines: CIB portfolio targets are global (core subsidiaries); SCF auto lending target covers European passenger cars across 16 units in 13 countries. Baseline years: 2019 (most sectors), 2020/2022 (auto manufacturing/auto lending), 2020 for own operations.
  - Financed emissions measurement: Applies PCAF methodologies; notes at least one-year data lag; supplements with sector-average factors for regulatory perimeters; includes equity and sovereign exposures where material.
  - Portfolio exposure: Approximately 9% of total lending (and ~18% of CIB lending) in sectors with published alignment targets (excluding thermal coal phase-out). PCAF membership since 2021.
- Cross-references: Each IRO links to relevant report sections on climate risk management, employees, customers, communities, suppliers, ethics/whistleblowing, and environmental/social risk processes, reinforcing integrated governance and accountability.

structure.title: Our transition plan
structure.heading: SN 4. Our transition plan
structure.start_phrase: Target types : To help our customers’ transition to a low-carbon economy, we employ physical emissions intensity for setting targets in the power generation, steel, aviation and auto sectors.
structure.summary:
- Outlines Santander’s transition plan and approach to setting portfolio alignment targets: physical emissions intensity for power, steel, aviation and autos; absolute emissions for oil & gas; prioritizes client engagement over divestment and evaluates cases individually to avoid unintended disincentives amid the absence of a universal transition finance taxonomy.
- Uses the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (IEA‑NZE) scenario to set 2030, 1.5°C‑aligned targets; aviation target based on expected adoption of current technologies. Own operations’ Scope 1 & 2 target follows SBTi’s cross‑sector absolute contraction (exceeding a 4.2% linear annual reduction).
- Provides scenario reference points for 2030 (e.g., power 0.19 tCO2/MWh; oil & gas −23% vs 2019; steel 1.29 tCO2e/t; aviation 60.59 gCO2e/RPK; autos 116 gCO2/vkm; own ops −42% vs 2020).
- Defines target coverage: CIB portfolio targets are global and include core subsidiaries; SCF target covers European passenger car loans and leases across 16 units (13 countries), with plans to extend to other vehicle types. Notes baseline years (2019 for initial sectors; 2020/2022 for autos) and that sectors with published targets represent ~9% of total lending and ~18% of CIB lending.
- Explains financed emissions methodology and disclosure: calculates according to PCAF, focused on high‑emitting, actionable value chain segments, with a data lag of at least one year; also estimates financed emissions for long‑term equity and sovereign debt holdings.
- Discloses financed emissions for alignment across sectors (power generation, oil & gas, aviation, steel, auto manufacturing, Brazil agriculture, European auto lending, UK/Spain mortgages and commercial real estate), including exposures, covered scopes, absolute emissions, physical and financial intensities, and PCAF data quality scores for 2020–2023.
- Details data quality and attribution: primary sources include CDP, Trucost, Asset Impact, TPI and company reports; for corporate loans, attribution uses Total Value of the Company (equity + debt) to reduce market cap volatility. Clarifies these calculations differ from EBA Pillar 3 perimeter and methods.
- States stance on internal carbon pricing: does not apply a standalone “fictitious” internal carbon price; instead integrates carbon cost assumptions in scenario analysis and transition risk tools and supports real‑economy carbon pricing. Offsets residual Scope 1 & 2 emissions via rigorously selected, independently rated carbon credits, with ongoing monitoring of the voluntary carbon market.
- Notes EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks: Santander is not excluded; exposure to undertakings excluded from these benchmarks is disclosed in Pillar 3.
- Provides EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures: reports Green Asset Ratio (GAR) of 3.04% (turnover‑based) and 3.28% (CapEx‑based); flow GAR of 2.6% and 3.4% respectively; eligibility for climate objectives at 34%. Highlights limitations—Taxonomy does not capture all transition‑supporting activities and numerator/denominator asymmetry excludes, for example, many SME and non‑European green loans.
- Assesses locked‑in GHG emissions: own direct emissions and key assets are not material sources of Scope 1 & 2; Scope 3 materiality is dominated by category 3.15 (financed emissions, >99% of Scope 3). Category 3.11 (use of sold products) is not material. Insufficient counterparty data currently prevents robust locked‑in estimates for category 3.15.

structure.title: EU Taxonomy
structure.heading: SN 5. EU Taxonomy
structure.start_phrase:
In 2020, the European Union adopted the Taxonomy Regulation
that sets out a list of activities that can qualify as environmentally
sustainable90 and stipulates that companies subject to the
Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD91) must disclose
how their operations align with the EU Taxonomy.
structure.summary:
- Describes Grupo Santander’s approach to managing its environmental impact, including reducing operational CO2e emissions (scopes 1 and 2) and offsetting residual emissions through rigorously selected, certified, and independently rated carbon credits, with active monitoring of the voluntary carbon market.
- Notes Santander’s inclusion under EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks and references disclosure of exposures to undertakings excluded from those benchmarks in Pillar 3 reports.
- Explains “locked‑in” GHG emissions: direct emissions and key assets’ scope 1 and 2 are not material; scope 3 financed emissions (category 3.15) account for over 99% of total scope 3; “use of sold products” (3.11) is not material; data gaps currently prevent reliable estimation of locked‑in financed emissions.
- Outlines EU Taxonomy Article 8/CSRD reporting, focusing on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), which measures financing of Taxonomy‑aligned activities versus total balance sheet.
- Reports 2024 GAR results: 3.04% (turnover‑based) and 3.28% (CapEx‑based), while noting Taxonomy limitations that understate transition efforts (e.g., asymmetric numerator/denominator, limited data such as energy efficiency certificates in some markets, and complex DNSH/MSS evidence requirements).
- Introduces a complementary “European & symmetric” GAR to address design limitations, with 2024 results of 7.90%, aligning numerator and denominator only to European, labelable exposures.
- Provides GAR/KPI disclosures for other businesses per European Commission requirements: asset management KPI 1.59% (turnover) and 2.60% (CapEx); insurance investment KPI 1.45% (turnover) and 2.05% (CapEx); investment services KPI deemed immaterial.
- Presents a consolidated KPI across businesses: 2.99% (turnover‑based) and 3.24% (CapEx‑based), weighted by revenue shares.
- Highlights that many transition‑supporting activities are not fully captured by current Taxonomy criteria (e.g., certain hybrids), and that data and implementation challenges reduce reported alignment.
- References where to find fuller disclosures, EU taxonomy templates, and links to the bank’s green transition support and GFANZ transition planning sections.
- Introduces the Sustainable Finance and Investment Classification System (SFICS), updated from 2022 guidelines and expanded in 2024 to include socially responsible investment standards, establishing Group‑wide criteria for classifying environmental, social, and sustainable activities.
- Notes SFICS alignment with international standards and principles (EU Taxonomy, ICMA, LMA, UNEP FI, Climate Bonds, Febraban) to enable tracking, product development, and greenwashing risk mitigation.
- Details SFICS updates: a customer‑based sustainability approach complementing activity‑based criteria; expanded sector guidance (manufacturing, real estate, sustainable agriculture, etc.); new activities covering water, waste, circular economy, and biodiversity goals.
- Describes eligible product types under SFICS: dedicated‑purpose (use‑of‑proceeds) financing and sustainability‑linked financing aligned with ICMA/LMA standards, supported by an updated (2023) global framework for green, social, and sustainability funding that governs use of proceeds, selection, management, and reporting.

structure.title: Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS)
structure.heading: SN 6. Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS)
structure.start_phrase: Sustainable finance is key to meeting our climate ambition.
structure.summary:
- The document excerpt is from the 2024 Annual Report’s Sustainability section, focusing on the Sustainable finance and investment classification system (SFICS) and a comprehensive set of performance tables.
- SFICS overview and purpose:
  - Introduced in 2022 and updated in 2024 to include socially responsible investment standards; now a Group-wide system to classify environmental, social and sustainable assets and activities.
  - Aims to track sustainable activity, guide product development, and mitigate greenwashing risk across all business units.
  - Draws on leading market standards and principles, including the EU Taxonomy (with 2023’s four new environmental objectives), ICMA and LMA principles, UNEP FI framework, Climate Bonds Standard, and Brazil’s Febraban taxonomy.
- Key 2024 enhancements to SFICS:
  - Adds a customer-focused sustainability approach to complement the activity-based approach.
  - Expands criteria for manufacturing, real estate, sustainable agriculture, and other sectors.
  - Incorporates new environmental goals on water, waste, circular economy and biodiversity, reflecting EU Taxonomy developments.
  - Commits to ongoing evolution to better classify green and transition activities in support of customer transitions and climate ambition.
- Eligible sustainable finance products and frameworks:
  - Use-of-proceeds instruments (green, social, sustainability bonds and loans) directed to eligible environmental and social activities aligned with ICMA/LMA, Climate Bonds Standard, and the EU Taxonomy.
  - Sustainability-linked financing aligned with ICMA/LMA, with structures tied to pre-defined ESG performance targets and metrics.
  - A 2023 updated, unified Green, Social and Sustainability Funding Global Framework governs all labelled funding across the Group, replacing prior global bond frameworks; it aligns with best practice on use of proceeds, project selection, management of proceeds, and reporting, and is consistent with SFICS.
- “Our progress in figures” (SN 7) outlines the metrics and disclosures to follow:
  - Green transition: green finance volumes, environmental footprint, Scopes 1–3 and total GHG emissions, carbon-credit-backed mitigation projects, and Equator Principles reporting.
  - EU Taxonomy tables.
  - Employees: breakdowns by region, gender, management group, age, contract type; collective bargaining and social dialogue; turnover; remuneration and ratios (including senior management and long-term incentive links); leadership composition; training; and occupational health and safety.
  - Customers: customer base, engagement channels, NPS rankings by country, and complaints.
  - Financial inclusion: number of people financially included and microfinance activity.
  - Community support: contributions, outputs and outcomes.
  - Tax contribution: total taxes paid.

  - Dismissals in 2024: 14,385; dismissal rate 6.9% (vs 6.7% in 2023); 53.9% women (aligned with workforce mix, down 3 pp vs 2023). Distribution: by management group (114 senior executives, 1,229 other executives, 13,042 other employees) and by age (<30: 4,495; 30–50: 7,866; >50: 2,024). Definitions clarify inclusions (e.g., reorganizations/redundancies, performance/disciplinary) and exclusions (e.g., temporary absences, intra-group transfers).
- SN 9 outlines additional Alternative Performance Measures (not additionally verified beyond limited assurance) and their purpose/sources:
  - Tax contribution metrics: taxes paid by the Group (e.g., corporate income tax, non-recoverable VAT, employer social security, sectoral charges), third-party taxes collected (withholdings, recoverable VAT, non-resident, property, stamp, financial activity taxes), and total tax contribution; references to SN 7.7 for data and emphasis on tax transparency.
  - Sustainable finance metrics and data sources: green finance raised and facilitated (tracked via league tables such as Infralogic, Bloomberg, Dealogic, TXF, Mergermarket), financing volumes for renewable energy projects, and electric vehicle financing; references to climate transition and sustainability sections.
  - Financial inclusion metric: credit disbursed to microentrepreneurs in Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru; references to related sections; highlights contribution to inclusion.
- Overall, the section documents regulatory workforce disclosures, dismissal analytics, and defines APMs for tax, green finance, and inclusion, with cross-references to detailed data elsewhere in the report.

structure.title: Alternative performance measures (APMs)
structure.heading: SN 9. Alternative performance measures (APMs)
structure.start_phrase:
The following are additional alternative performance measures
(APMs) to those listed in section 8 of the chapter 'Economic and
Financial Review' .
structure.summary:
- Excerpt from Santander’s 2024 Annual Report detailing additional Alternative Performance Measures (APMs) for sustainability reporting (SN 9) and the Non‑financial Information Act 11/2018 content index (SN 10), noting metrics are only subject to limited assurance.
- Tax contribution metrics: definitions and scope for taxes paid by the Group, third‑party taxes collected, and total tax contribution, reinforcing tax transparency by geography.
- Sustainable finance metrics: 
  - Green finance raised and facilitated across products (project finance, advisory, bonds, ECAs, M&A, ECM) aligned to ESG classifications and external league tables.
  - Financing volumes for renewable energy projects and fully electric vehicles.
  - Credit disbursed to microentrepreneurs in Latin America, evidencing financial inclusion.
- Financed emissions methodologies aligned mainly to PCAF:
  - Corporates and projects: attribution factor formulas, company value basis (equity + debt), project production x emission factors, and multiple external data sources.
  - Auto lending (SCF Europe): loan‑level attribution and vehicle‑specific emissions based on estimated annual distance.
  - Mortgages and Commercial Real Estate: Scope 1 and 2 using actual/modelled EPCs, with emissions attributed via LTV.
  - Agriculture (Brazil): Scope 1 and 2 with GHG Protocol/PCAF adaptations; land management and land‑use change emissions using farm shapefiles, MapBiomas, national inventories, and linear discounting; bank attribution applied.
  - Sovereign bonds: exposure/GDP‑PPP x national emissions.
- Responsible investment: definition of SRI Assets Under Management per SFDR Articles 8 and 9 (plus equivalents in non‑SFDR markets), including SAM, other Group managers, third‑party funds, and SFICS criteria.
- Employee training: definition of total training investment covering internal/external delivery, logistics, labour, IT, and communication costs.
- Community support: measures for investments in education, employability and entrepreneurship, other local initiatives (social welfare, culture), and the total community support figure.
- Suppliers: total payments to suppliers and percentage of turnover with locally contracted suppliers, reflecting local economic contribution.
- Extensive cross‑references to where underlying data and tables appear elsewhere in the report.
- SN 10 content index: mapping of Spain’s Act 11/2018 disclosure requirements to report sections and their correspondence with CSRD/ESRS:
  - Business model overview, environment, markets, strategies, and trends.
  - Policies and due diligence (including human rights and ESG risk integration).
  - Results with KPIs enabling monitoring and comparability.
  - Principal impacts, risks, and opportunities, and how they are identified and managed over different time horizons.

structure.title: Non-financial information Act 11/2018 content index
structure.heading: SN 10. Non-financial information Act 11/2018 content index
structure.start_phrase:
Detailed information on the current and foreseeable effects 
of the activities of the company in the environment and,
where appropriate, health and safety, environmental
evaluation or certification procedures; the resources
dedicated to the prevention of environmental risks; the
application of the principle of caution, the amount of
provisions and guarantees for environmental risks.
structure.summary:
- Crosswalk/index linking Spain’s Act 11/2018 non-financial reporting requirements to Banco Santander’s 2024 Annual Report sections, with correspondence to CSRD/ESRS and other regulations.
- Business model and strategy: description of the group’s environment, organization, markets, objectives, strategy, and trends; materiality assessment and methodology.
- Policies and due diligence: sustainability governance, human rights due diligence, embedding ESG in business and risk management; procedures to identify, assess, prevent, mitigate, verify, and control impacts.
- Results and KPIs: progress indicators and comparable metrics across environmental, social, and governance areas (“Our progress in figures”).
- Risks, impacts, and opportunities: main short-, medium-, and long-term ESG risks related to activities, products, and services; detection/assessment procedures and management approach.
- Environment: environmental footprint; pollution (including air, noise, light); circular economy and waste; sustainable resource use (water, raw materials); energy consumption, efficiency, and renewables; climate change (GHG emissions, adaptation measures, reduction targets); biodiversity approach; statement of no significant environmental provisions/guarantees at 2023 year-end.
- Social and employment: workforce composition by gender/age/country/classification; contract types; dismissals; remuneration levels and progression; gender pay gap and equal pay; executive pay by gender; right to disconnect; disability inclusion.
- Working conditions and H&S: work organization, absences, work-life balance measures; health and safety conditions; accident frequency/severity and occupational illnesses by gender.
- Social relations: social dialogue, collective bargaining coverage, H&S in agreements; worker involvement in company management.
- Training: policies and total training hours by category; employee feedback and experience; ethical reporting channels.
- Accessibility and equality: universal accessibility; equal treatment measures; anti-harassment and anti-discrimination protocols; diversity management; community support.
- Human rights: due diligence application; prevention/mitigation/remediation of abuses; complaints handling; adherence to ILO conventions (freedom of association, collective bargaining, non-discrimination, no forced/child labor).
- Conduct, compliance, and anti-financial crime: anti-corruption/bribery; anti–money laundering; compliance risk management; contributions to non-profits.
- Communities, customers, and suppliers: community development and financial inclusion; stakeholder engagement and sector associations; customer health/safety and complaints; responsible procurement with social/gender/environmental criteria; supplier oversight and audits.
- Tax and transparency: country-by-country results; corporate taxes paid; disclosure on public subsidies (none significant in 2023/2024).
- EU Taxonomy: Article 8 disclosures and responsible investment/social finance.
- ESRS content index: references for ESRS 2 general disclosures (basis of preparation); governance (roles of administrative/management/supervisory bodies, information flows, incentives tied to sustainability, due diligence statement, and internal controls over sustainability reporting) with page citations.

structure.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 on sustainability reporting standards content index
structure.heading: SN 11. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 on sustainability reporting standards content index
structure.start_phrase:
Table with references to sections and subsections of the Sustainability statement that respond to the information
requirements of the Directive (EU) 2022/2464 of the European Parliament and the Commission Delegated Regulation
(EU) 2023/2772.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: An ESRS/CSRD content index for Santander’s Annual Report 2024 that maps each European Sustainability Reporting Standard (per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772) to the exact sections, subsections, sustainability notes, and tables where the required disclosures are addressed.

- General disclosures (ESRS 2): Basis for preparation (BP-1, BP-2) and disclosures in special circumstances, with cross-references to “About this chapter” and Sustainability Notes (SN 1).

- Governance: Roles of administrative, management and supervisory bodies (GOV-1 to GOV-5), integration of sustainability performance in incentives, due diligence (including human rights), and controls over sustainability reporting. References include “1.4 Sustainability governance,” SN 2, and related employee and senior management composition tables.

- Strategy and business model: SBM-1 to SBM-3 covering sustainability strategy, value chain, stakeholder engagement, and material impacts/risks/opportunities and their interaction with strategy. Notes a non-material revenue share for certain sectors (1.46%). Points to detailed materiality methodology (SN 3) and ties to sections on customers, communities, and green transition.

- Materiality assessment and IRO: Processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO-1), and how ESRS disclosure requirements are covered (IRO-2), with detailed methodology in SN 3 and an index in SN 11.

- Minimum Disclosure Requirements (MDR): Policies (MDR-P), actions/resources (MDR-A), metrics (MDR-M), and targets (MDR-T) linked to climate transition, employees/communities/customers, business conduct, and alternative performance measures (SN 9).

- Climate change (ESRS E1):
  - Governance: Incentive integration (ESRS 2 GOV-3).
  - Strategy: Transition plan (E1-1), alignment with Paris Agreement, client transition support, and enabling policies (2.1–2.5; SN 4).
  - Risk management: Identification/assessment processes (ESRS 2 IRO-1), resilience, risk cycle, and potential financial effects (phase-in for certain items).
  - Metrics and targets: Climate targets (E1-4), energy consumption/mix (E1-5), GHG emissions Scopes 1–3 and total (E1-6), GHG removals and credits (E1-7), internal carbon pricing (E1-8), anticipated financial effects of physical/transition risks and opportunities (E1-9). Includes environmental footprint and emissions tables (SN 7.1). Notes related governance/policy frameworks (Sustainability Governance, SFICS, ESCC).

- Nature and other environmental standards: Linkages to ESRS E2–E5 via the ESG risk management process.

- Own workforce (ESRS S1):
  - Policies, engagement, remediation/grievance channels, actions and effectiveness across talent/skills, working conditions, inclusion, and employee feedback.
  - Metrics and targets: Headcount by region/gender/contract, turnover, collective bargaining coverage, diversity (management group, age), adequate wages, social protection, disability inclusion, training hours, health and safety, pay gap and compensation ratios. Reliance on ESRS phase-in for some non-employee data. References to SN 7.3 metric tables and ethical channels (“Canal Abierto”).

- Affected communities (ESRS S3):
  - Strategy and IRO: Stakeholder engagement, policies, remediation channels, actions/effectiveness tied to responsible investment and social finance, ESG/climate management, and community support. Notes pending definitions for types of affected communities and additional governance details in sustainability governance sections.

- Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4):
  - Policies, engagement, remediation channels, actions/effectiveness regarding customer conduct, financial inclusion/health, and privacy/data protection/cybersecurity, with associated targets.

- Business conduct (ESRS G1):
  - Governance and IRO processes, corporate culture and policies, supplier relationship management, anti-corruption and bribery prevention/detection.
  - Metrics: Confirmed corruption/bribery incidents and payment practices. References include ethical conduct, financial crime compliance, suppliers, and materiality sections.

- Financial impacts and notes: Indicates potential financial impacts from identified risks (legal claims, penalties) with references to annual accounts Notes 25.d) and 25.e).

- Cross-referencing architecture: Consistent pointers to core chapters—1. Sustainability at Santander; 2. Our climate transition plan; 3. Supporting employees, communities and customers; 4. Business conduct; Sustainability Notes (SN 1–11), and specific data tables (environmental footprint, emissions, training, remuneration, etc.).

- Assurance: Concludes with an Independent Verification Report.
